title: "It's Like You're Trying to Defuse a Bomb": Fear, Responsibility, and Shame in Young Men's Sexual Lives
one_line: Thematic analysis of 31 single-sitting interviews (64-124 min, mean 92) with heterosexual men aged 18-32, conducted in late 2023, reporting that these men who grew up inside consent-focused sex education rarely described enjoying sex.
key_claims: Anxiety and vigilance: 29 of 31 men (94%) spontaneously described fear, nervousness or pressure around sex, and the same 29 described it shaping behaviour through constant monitoring of a partner's signals and of themselves.

Fear of causing harm: also 29 of 31, substantially overlapping the first group, with the authors arguing the concern tips into people-pleasing and self-erasure — men describing unenthusiastic sex performed for a partner's benefit, one handing over 'full control', which the authors note could protect him as much as please her.

Shame: 26 of 31 (84%) described sex as high stakes, of whom 19 (61%) feared formal consequences such as accusation, legal trouble or career damage, 17 (55%) feared informal consequences such as gossip, reputation and exclusion, and 16 (52%) turned the same logic inward.

The inward turn is the thesis: men judged themselves rather than only their partner's wishes as the uncertain, risky object — 'am I the kind of man who could get this wrong' — which the authors read as internalised cultural suspicion and tie to the shame-versus-guilt distinction, guilt prompting change where shame prevents it.

The emotional material was not what the study sought: the seven-question guide never asks how sex feels, and the themes came from spontaneous asides noticed during fieldwork, after which all 31 transcripts were coded line by line.

The authors argue these men overestimate the likelihood of a false accusation, citing a Law Commission report and Victoria Police data rather than anything in this dataset, and state their finding is about the fear, not its frequency.
limitations: Four of the seven interview questions point at uncertain or non-consensual encounters and none asks about pleasure or good sex, so the headline claim — an absence of described enjoyment — is exactly what this instrument would manufacture; the authors flag it but in a single paragraph.

The percentages are counts of spontaneous mention in one cohort, not prevalence: non-mention was deliberately not treated as absence, and the authors state in as many words that the counts describe this cohort only.

Self-selected volunteers for a consent study with a 40-dollar grocery voucher, 26 of 35 recruited by campus flyers at mostly one Australian university and 9 by snowballing, 24 in Australia and 7 in the US, 5 interviews in Spanish, men charged or convicted of a sexual offence ineligible — so the sample skews toward men who already think about consent a lot.
Performance anxiety could not be separated from consent-related anxiety; the authors say the two were hard to disentangle for these men and do not disentangle them either.
Accounts of social exclusion mix real and imagined cases and the paper cannot separate them.
One participant, 'Ernest', 28, is quoted more than anyone, which the methods disclose, so the reader's impression of 31 men is set disproportionately by one articulate one.

One interview each, no partners interviewed, mostly Judeo-Christian upbringing; the discussion nonetheless suggests the pattern may reach young men across Western post-MeToo societies, which sits uneasily with the stated sampling limits.
open_questions: Run the same study with a guide that includes pleasure and good encounters, and ideally young women on the same schedule, to test whether the inward turn is specific to these men.
Measure shame and self-criticism on a validated scale alongside interviews in a sample not recruited to talk about consent.
Test the shame-versus-guilt interpretation directly, since the authors present it as an interpretation and it is testable.
Separate consent-related anxiety from ordinary sexual performance anxiety with a design that asks about both.
